docs.title: Citation and Ethics
docs.text: Accurate citation is both an academic standard and an ethical practice.

docs.title: Core Principles
docs.text:
• Give credit for ideas, phrasing, data, and visuals.
  • Distinguish between summary, paraphrase, and quotation.
  • Use one citation style consistently.

docs.title: Ethical Risks to Avoid
docs.text:
• Patchwriting without attribution
  • Misrepresenting evidence context
  • Selective citation that distorts meaning
  • Omitting source limitations

docs.title: Citation Workflow
docs.text:
1. Capture source details immediately.
  2. Keep notes separate from draft text.
  3. Mark direct quotations clearly.
  4. Verify in-text and bibliography consistency before submission.

docs.title: Slide Storytelling
docs.text: Slides should support your message, not compete with it.

docs.title: Story Arc for Presentations
docs.text:
• Setup: define context and stakes
  • Tension: show the challenge or gap
  • Resolution: present findings and recommendation

docs.title: Slide Design Principles
docs.text:
• One idea per slide
  • High-contrast visuals and short text
  • Consistent typographic hierarchy
  • Intentional pacing with transitions

docs.title: Speaker Alignment
docs.text:
1. Use slides as cues, not scripts.
  2. Place detail in spoken delivery or handouts.
  3. End with a clear action or takeaway.

docs.title: Audience Analysis
docs.text: Audience analysis helps you shape content before drafting.

docs.title: Key Questions
docs.text:
• Who will read or hear this?
  • What background knowledge do they already have?
  • What concerns, values, or goals matter most to them?
  • What action should they take after engaging with your work?

docs.title: Practical Method
docs.text:
1. Define primary and secondary audiences.
  2. List what each audience knows, believes, and needs.
  3. Adjust tone, examples, and detail depth for each audience.
  4. Validate your assumptions with feedback.

docs.title: Source Evaluation
docs.text: Evaluating sources protects your argument quality and credibility.

docs.title: CRAAP-Inspired Criteria
docs.text:
• Currency: Is the source recent enough for your topic?
  • Relevance: Does it directly support your claim?
  • Authority: Is the author or publisher credible?
  • Accuracy: Are methods and references transparent?
  • Purpose: Is there bias, sponsorship, or agenda?

docs.title: Cross-Check Routine
docs.text:
1. Verify author expertise.
  2. Confirm publication context.
  3. Compare with at least two additional reliable sources.
  4. Save citation details as you read.

docs.title: Red Flags
docs.text:
• No author identity
  • No references or weak evidence
  • Sensational language without data
  • Claims that cannot be independently verified

docs.title: Revision Strategy
docs.text: Revision is where clarity, structure, and persuasion improve most.

docs.title: Three-Pass Model
docs.text:
1. Structural pass: sequence and section logic
  2. Argument pass: evidence quality and claim alignment
  3. Sentence pass: style, concision, and correctness

docs.title: Revision Questions
docs.text:
• Does each section have a clear purpose?
  • Are transitions guiding the reader?
  • Is evidence interpreted, not just inserted?
  • Are there repeated words or filler phrases?

docs.title: Fast Improvement Tactics
docs.text:
• Read aloud to catch rhythm and ambiguity.
  • Convert passive constructions where clarity suffers.
  • Replace abstract language with concrete terms.
  • Cut one sentence from every paragraph if possible.

docs.title: Thesis Development
docs.text: A thesis is the central claim that your writing proves.

docs.title: Strong Thesis Checklist
docs.text:
• Specific: avoids vague wording
  • Arguable: reasonable people could disagree
  • Focused: supports a clear scope
  • Significant: explains why the claim matters

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
Claim + Reason + Stakes

Example:

Integrating visual evidence in technical reports improves decision quality because it reduces interpretation ambiguity for mixed-expertise teams.

docs.title: Revision Steps
docs.text:
1. Underline your core claim.
  2. Remove extra ideas not tied to that claim.
  3. Add context about impact and relevance.
  4. Test whether each body paragraph supports the thesis.
